title: The quotient and remainder of a division are unique
statement: If n = d*q1 + r1 with r1 < d and n = d*q2 + r2 with r2 < d, then q1 = q2 and r1 = r2.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.div_mod_unique : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat) -> ((x3 : AxNat) -> ((x4 : AxNat) -> ((x5 : AxNat) -> ((x6 : AxNat.divMod x0 x1 x2 x3) -> ((x7 : AxNat.divMod x0 x1 x4 x5) -> And (Eq.{1} AxNat x2 x4) (Eq.{1} AxNat x3 x5)))))))))

evidence.notes: `nat_axiom_inventory` enumerates the built Nat environment and reports `nat: axiom=0 opaque=0 quotient=0 total_trusted=0` (re-run 2026-08-14 by this lane). That is the whole environment, not this theorem, and that is what makes it sound as a footprint: a theorem cannot depend on a trusted declaration the environment does not contain, so an empty trusted surface bounds every individual footprint by []. Counting `Declaration::Axiom` alone would NOT have sufficed -- `Opaque` has no proof body and `Quotient` admits `Quot.sound`, one of Lean's own axioms -- so the enumeration covers all three.

notes: Uniqueness is the other half of the division algorithm, and it is what makes `Nat.div` and `Nat.mod` well defined rather than merely one choice among several. depends_on records the mathematical prerequisite, not a measured proof-term footprint. formal.statement is the type the kernel admitted, taken verbatim from Kernel::render_lean over the environment build_nat_prelude produces; it was not transcribed by hand. The sort renders as `AxNat` (the prelude's own inductive) while declarations are rooted at `Nat`.
